s11.slug: THURSDAY · 9:00 PM · THE FRONT ROOM → THE PORCH
s11.music: Ella Fitzgerald — “What Are You Doing New Year’s Eve?”
body: At ten to nine the VCR under the television is rewinding with its little motor whining, and Ma has put a CD in the player on top of the console stereo to cover the sound of it, and turned the lamp off so the tree can have the room. The tape lives on top of the VCR all year in a cardboard sleeve, and the label says, in Ma’s capitals: TIMES SQ. 12-31-99 — DO NOT TAPE OVER — FRANK THIS MEANS YOU.

Rosie’s midnight is at nine. It has been at nine since Gina was small enough to fall asleep in a paper hat, and it has been this tape since the real millennium, when Frank sat up with a blank cassette in the machine and his thumb over RECORD so the kids could have it after. Jack did midnight at nine off it till he was twelve and too old for it, and then he was the one who ran the VCR. Tonight it’s Gina’s job. She has the remote in one hand and Theo’s Flip in the other, and has told everyone twice that she is shooting a documentary and nobody is to look at the camera.

Rosie is standing on the coffee table, allowed tonight and no other night of the year, in her pajamas and her church shoes, with Ma’s saucepan in one hand and a wooden spoon in the other. Nonna is in her chair by the window with her beads and a pot lid in her lap. Frank is on the couch. Ma stands in the kitchen doorway with the dish towel over her shoulder, where she can watch the tape and the stove both.

The tape clunks at the start and plays. It’s ten years ago in Times Square: a million people with their breath going up in the lights, kids on their fathers’ shoulders in novelty glasses shaped like 2000, and Dick Clark telling all of them how long they’ve got. The picture rolls once where the tape has gotten tired. Rosie doesn’t care. When the crowd on the screen starts counting she counts with it at the top of her lungs, and the front room counts along with a crowd ten years gone — Gina behind the Flip, Frank low from the couch, Ma from the doorway — and Nonna half a number behind all of them in Italian, *sette, sei, cinque*, coming in under the English, as she does at the rosary. At zero the ball comes down and the 2000 under it lights up, and 1999 throws its hats in the air, and Rosie hits the saucepan so hard the spoon flies out of her hand and into the tree.

For the porch, Ma has the pots out on the radiator by the front door, the same pots every year: the spaghetti pot and its lid, the cast-iron that only Frank can lift with one hand, two saucepans, and the colander for Gina, who likes the sound. Frank turns Nonna’s chair around to face the door and opens it wide, and Nonna sits in the cold coming in with her coat over her knees and the pot lid held up, ready. Everybody else goes out.

Glenwood is frozen hard and empty under the streetlights, and the moon is up over the roofs across the street, full, so bright the salt on the walk throws little shadows. In the side yard the Madonna stands blue in her tub under Frank’s lights. Rosie goes first, on the top step, beating the saucepan at the street, and then all of them: Ma on the spaghetti pot, Frank on the cast-iron with the spoon going like he’s mad at it, Gina on the colander with the Flip held out in her other hand, and behind them in the open door Nonna’s lid, *ding, ding, ding*, a little off the beat. Two doors up, past the Santa still lying on his face in the yard, a porch light comes on and somebody bangs back. Somebody further down the block answers on what has to be a hubcap.
“It’s a blue moon,” Gina tells Rosie between bangs. “Second full one in a month.”
Rosie stops banging to look up at it. She looks for some time. “It’s not *blue*.”
“It’s an expression.”
Rosie goes back to the saucepan, without the same heart in it.

Inside, Ma has the Asti out of the refrigerator and the little juice glasses on a tray: a finger in each for her and Nonna and Jack, a finger for Gina, who gets a look with it, and grape juice for Rosie in a real wine glass, because she asked for one in October. Frank’s is a ginger ale, in a glass. He lifts it.
“Everybody,” he says, and they drink.
Ma looks at the glass in his hand, and then at the tree, and drinks her Asti.
Gina has the Flip up again with the red light on. “The Costigan New Year Documentary,” she announces. “Resolutions. One line each. No speeches, *Ma*.”

Frank, on the couch, into the lens: “Browns.” Ma, from the doorway: “Everybody eats.” Gina swings it to the window, and Nonna leans in close to the little camera and tells it something in Calabrese, at length, with one finger up, and sits back satisfied. “I’m not translating that,” Gina says. “That’s for the extras.” Rosie, from the coffee table, with grape juice on her lip: “Another crab.”
Then the camera comes around to Jack on the end of the couch, and the little red light waits on him.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first. Friday morning, a voicemail: Browns beat Pittsburgh. Thirteen–six. Eight sacks. Thought I’d want to know. Christmas: waited at the bottom of the escalator in Pittsburgh with a thermos and asked about the girl, because Ma told him to. Ginger ale at the bar, in a glass. Stayed in the truck at Trumbull — the twenty-seventh, he says. Drove Theo and me up Christmas Eve and stayed in the truck again. Told Theo Danny ate everything at eleven. Two-eighty-six. Gave Theo the parka without a word. “You’re not company.” Held the 1964 program a long time. On Skye: “Huh.” Asked me what it’s like in there. Went in on Holy Family Sunday — his name was on the list at the desk; he asked Ma where he’s supposed to stand. Told Danny they wouldn’t lose. Three straight. His phone died in the cold and he borrowed mine. New Year’s: a ginger ale, in a glass.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs. Put season two in the DVD player the day after Christmas, for research, and the whole family watched. Wrote Danny about the boat. It’s a yacht. Filmed everybody’s resolutions on Theo’s Flip.

journal.title: Rosie
journal.text: Rosie Costigan, eight. Drew Theo as a prince before she ever met him. Drew him again in Dad’s parka. He kept both. Christmas Eve she said grace — the baby in New Orleans, Danny, Nonna’s hand, Theo’s mom’s coach. Christmas night she drew the TV girl, with me and a crab. Rosie’s midnight is at nine, off a tape Dad made in 1999. Pots and pans on the porch. Asleep by a quarter past with the spoon.

response: “Say things out loud,” Jack says.
Gina lowers the camera and looks at him over the top of it, and raises it again. “That’s a weird one.” It’s on tape.

By a quarter past nine Rosie is asleep at the end of the couch with her feet in her father’s lap and the wooden spoon still in her fist. Frank runs the tape back to the beginning with the sound off and watches the crowd do it all again, his hand around her ankle. Through the rest of the evening the phone goes in Jack’s pocket.

response.text: Respectfully, happy new year. I am at my aunt’s in San Jose. Forty people. One bathroom.

s11a.slug: THURSDAY · 10:25 PM · A BASEMENT ON THE SOUTH SIDE
body: Ryan Pallante’s basement is knotty-pine paneling and a drop ceiling with a water stain in the shape of Ohio, a bar his father built from a kit the year Ryan was born, a dryer with a cooler of ice on top of it, and a sheet of plywood across two sawhorses for beer pong. Somebody’s iPod sits in a dock on the bar playing something with a great deal of synthesizer in it that three girls from Ursuline know every word of. There are forty people down here, and Jack went to grade school or Mooney or CYO with most of them, and the rest are somebody’s cousin. Upstairs Mrs. Pallante has a ham out on the kitchen table under foil, and every half hour she comes to the top of the stairs to tell the room there’s ham.

Ryan sees him at the bottom of the stairs and comes through the crowd with both arms up. Ryan is the boy who learned everybody’s middle name off the program at Mooney’s graduation and has used them ever since, at volume. “John *Anthony* Costigan! *California!*” He takes the pizzelles and passes them back over his shoulder to somebody, and the room turns around. “You see any movie stars out there?”
“One,” Jack says.
And the basement laughs, because it’s a joke. Ryan yells *ONE* at the drop ceiling like a final score, and somebody puts a beer in Jack’s hand.

It’s a Rolling Rock out of the cooler on the dryer, and he makes it last. Ryan himself is drinking Cherry Coke out of the can, because he has two cousins to drive home to Boardman at one o’clock, and he tells that to everybody who offers him anything, as if it’s news.

Tommy Hritz is here from St. Christine’s, the size of a refrigerator now, who broke Jack’s nose in the third quarter of the eighth-grade CYO game that Jack started. He comes over and shakes Jack’s hand like it was a long time ago, which it was, and studies the nose.
“Healed crooked.”
“You did good work.”
Tommy seems pleased with that, and goes back to the beer pong.

By the bar the Mooney kids have gotten around to Mr. Tomko, who taught them theology sophomore year, and somebody does him for Jack — the glasses pushed up on the forehead, the finger — “*Mister* Costigan. You will not out-Catholic me in my own classroom.” Jack got a detention for that one, for arguing the Pope’s side better than the textbook did, and served it, and served the six-thirty Mass the next morning anyway. Half the room calls him Costigan and the other half calls him Jack, and two girls from St. Brigid’s still call him Jackie, from the first grade, and he lets them.
Ryan’s cousin Bobby, who was a year behind Danny at Mooney and played JV with him, gets Jack by the furnace for a minute, away from the music.
“How’s Danny doing?”
“He’s good. He reads.”
Bobby nods at that. He says to tell him Bobby says hey, and that’s as far as he takes it, and they go back to the room.
Across the basement, by the beer pong, Carly Benedetto in the white knit hat catches his eye and raises her cup to him.

At eleven Mrs. Pallante comes down the stairs herself with a ham sandwich on a paper plate, and a pickle, and finds him in the crowd by the bar, and puts it in his hands. “Your mother called,” she says. “Half past nine. She says you didn’t eat.”
“I ate twice.”

“She said you’d say that.” Mrs. Pallante watches him take the first bite. Then she picks the pizzelle plate up off the dryer, empty now except for the plastic wrap, and holds it up at him. “And you tell her I don’t have her platter. I never had her platter. You tell her look in her own cupboard over the refrigerator.” And she goes back up the stairs with the plate, to the ham.

The iPod goes from the synthesizers to Springsteen and back. A girl from Latin Club wants to know if it’s true they surf at his school, before class, and is disappointed in his answer. A boy who backed him up at point guard wants him in on the next game. Somebody’s little brother came down the stairs an hour ago and ate the pizzelles off the dryer one after another, and is now asleep under the bar.

At twenty-five to twelve Mrs. Pallante has the TV in the kitchen up loud enough that Times Square comes down the stairs, and down here a girl from Boardman with a voice built for running things is going around the room with a napkin and a pen, organizing who kisses whom at midnight. She is working her way down the paneling toward his end of it.

choices.key: New Year’s Eve you went to Ryan Pallante’s basement with the kids from Mooney, and stayed for midnight.
New Year’s Eve you went to Ryan Pallante’s basement with the kids from Mooney, and walked home for Nonna’s midnight.

s12a.slug: FRIDAY · 12:00 AM · RYAN’S → THE BACK STEPS
body: At a minute to twelve Ryan puts the Killers on and turns the dock up till the bar buzzes, and the whole basement sings it at the drop ceiling with their heads back, forty people who know every word, so that when Mrs. Pallante yells down the stairs that it’s on, the countdown comes down underneath the song from the kitchen TV and they have to count over it. *Ten.* The girl from Boardman has her napkin out. *Nine.* People are finding each other across the beer pong. Somewhere around the eight Jack is through the laundry room, and at the six he’s on the back stairs, and the back door lets him out into the night at about the two. Behind it the year turns over, muffled, in forty voices and one song.
Carly Benedetto is already out here, on the top step with her coat pulled around her and her knees up, smoking. She looks up at the door, and at him, and moves over to make room.
“Happy New Year,” she says.
“Happy New Year.”
He sits. In his coat the phone goes against his ribs, and again, and a third time.
“Go ahead,” Carly says. “Everybody’s got somebody.”
He opens it. There are three from midnight, all at once.

body.text: Your midnight. Happy New Year, Youngstown. Ours is an hour off. Mémère is lining us up at the door in church clothes so the year can see we tried. —L.

body: Theo’s he leaves for the walk home. He shuts the phone, and puts it away, and Carly is watching the yard.
Carly holds her pack out to him, Marlboro Lights, the same as junior year.
“I quit.”
“Since when?”
“I’m tapering.”
Carly laughs with the smoke still in her and has to cough it out, and puts the pack away.
Two yards over somebody has set a fountain off in the snow, and it spits green at the dark, and then gold. The moon is so bright he can tell her breath from her smoke.
“Ryan does this every year,” she says. “Every year his mother does the ham. Every year Bobby gets sick in the laundry sink, and every year he says it was the ham.”

She’s at YSU now, living at home, with chemistry at eight in the morning from a man who calls the roll by last names. “He calls me Benedetto. Like a sergeant. I said it’s Miss Benedetto. He said not in his room it isn’t.” Her mother is asleep in the recliner in front of the TV with her rosary in her lap. “She’ll wake up at one and tell me she saw the ball. She hasn’t seen the ball since Reagan.”
“You look like California,” she says.
“Fog. The whole time.”
“Still.”

She smokes. Over their heads in the kitchen Mrs. Pallante is laughing at somebody. Carly is watching the swing set at the back of the yard, which has a ridge of snow along the top bar and a seat hanging by one chain.
“Do you ever hear how Mikey’s mom is doing?”
The fountain two yards over burns down to the cardboard and quits, and whoever lit it says *aw*. Carly has turned to look at him with the cigarette halfway to her mouth, and it stops there.
“Jack. You okay? You went white.”
His hands are on the iron rail. He takes them off it and puts them in the pockets of the Carhartt.
She looks back out at the yard. “She goes to the nine-thirty at St. Nicholas,” Carly says. “In Struthers. She sits in the back.”
Inside, the song ends, and somebody starts it over. Carly smokes the cigarette down until there’s nothing left of it but filter, and looks at the filter.
“I go sometimes,” she says. “I sit behind her.”

journal.title: Carly Benedetto
journal.text: Mooney ’09, YSU now. Two pews up at Midnight Mass with her mother. Gave me the peace. Asked me to a thing at Ryan’s on New Year’s. New Year’s at Ryan Pallante’s, his mother’s basement. After midnight she was out on the back steps with a cigarette, and so was I.

choices.key: After midnight on New Year’s, Carly asked you about someone in Struthers. You told her you don’t hear.
response: “No,” he says. “I don’t.”
Carly nods, like it’s the answer she came out here with, and puts the cigarette out on the rail.

She goes back in after that, and the song comes out the door with her and goes back in when it shuts. He stays out on the steps until his ears ache. At twenty to one he goes down them and around the side of the house and starts home across the South Side, under a moon bright enough to lay his shadow out on the salt ahead of him.

choices.key: After midnight on New Year’s, Carly asked you about someone in Struthers. You asked how she is.
response: “How is she?”
“Tired,” Carly says. “She’s always tired.” Down in the basement they’ve started counting backward from ten again, for somebody who missed it. “She lights a candle after. Every week.”

She goes back in after that, and the song comes out the door with her and goes back in when it shuts. He stays out on the steps until his ears ache. At twenty to one he goes down them and around the side of the house and starts home across the South Side, under a moon bright enough to lay his shadow out on the salt ahead of him.

response: “Happy New Year, Carly.”
She lets him have it. “Happy New Year, Jack.” She doesn’t look at him when she says it.

She goes back in after that, and the song comes out the door with her and goes back in when it shuts. He stays out on the steps until his ears ache. At twenty to one he goes down them and around the side of the house and starts home across the South Side, under a moon bright enough to lay his shadow out on the salt ahead of him.

s12b.slug: THURSDAY · 11:40 PM · THE SIDEWALKS, THE SOUTH SIDE
body: At twenty to twelve he goes up the stairs past the ham, tells Mrs. Pallante happy New Year and that his mother wants her platter, and lets himself out the front door with Ryan yelling *JOHN ANTHONY, IT’S NOT MIDNIGHT* up the stairwell after him. Carly Benedetto is on the front walk ahead of him, pulling on her gloves. She’s leaving too.
“My mother wants me home by midnight,” she says. “She’s Slovak about it.”

The Benedettos are St. Brigid’s people, two streets over from Glenwood. It’s the same walk. They take it down the middle of the sidewalk under the full moon, which is high now and so bright the parked cars have shadows, and every house they pass has its television going behind the curtains on the same channel, so that Times Square comes out of one house and goes back into the next. When a car comes along they step off onto the lawns, and the snow crust creaks under their boots.
Halfway down the first block she lights a cigarette, Marlboro Lights, the same as junior year, and holds the pack out to him.
“I quit.”
“Since when?”
“I’m tapering.”

Carly laughs with the smoke still in her and has to cough it out at the moon. She’s at YSU now, living at home, with chemistry at eight in the morning from a man who calls the roll by last names. “He calls me Benedetto. Like a sergeant. I said it’s Miss Benedetto. He said not in his room it isn’t.” Her mother was asleep in the recliner by ten with her rosary in her lap. “She’ll tell me tomorrow she saw the ball. She hasn’t seen the ball since Reagan.” And Ryan’s party is the same every year, she says: the ham, the Killers at midnight, and Bobby sick in the laundry sink by one, swearing it was the ham. “Give him an hour.”
“You look like California,” she says.
“Fog. The whole time.”
“Still.”
Up ahead, at the corner where she turns off, her mother’s porch light is on. Carly has her eyes on it.
“Do you ever hear how Mikey’s mom is doing?”
Three more steps, and then she stops on the sidewalk, because he isn’t beside her. She turns around.
“Jack? You okay? You went white.”
His hands are in the pockets of the Carhartt, as far down as they go. A block back, somebody’s storm door bangs, and a party comes out of it and goes back in.
She waits for him to come up even with her, and then she says it walking again, with her eyes up the street. “She goes to the nine-thirty at St. Nicholas. In Struthers. She sits in the back.”
At the corner Carly stops to work her glove down tighter at the wrist.
“I go sometimes,” she says. “I sit behind her.”

journal.title: Carly Benedetto
journal.text: Mooney ’09, YSU now. Two pews up at Midnight Mass with her mother. Gave me the peace. Asked me to a thing at Ryan’s on New Year’s. New Year’s at Ryan Pallante’s, his mother’s basement. She walked home the same way at twenty to twelve — the Benedettos are two streets over from us.

“Tired,” Carly says. “She’s always tired.” Up the street the Benedettos’ front door opens, and her father’s voice says *Carly* once, the length of the block. “She lights a candle after. Every week.”
She turns off up her street.

response: “Happy New Year, Carly.”
“Happy New Year, Jack.” Not looking at him. She turns off up her street.

s12c.slug: THURSDAY · 11:58 PM · GLENWOOD AVENUE, THE FRONT ROOM
s12c.music: Guy Lombardo and His Royal Canadians — “Auld Lang Syne”
body: He comes in the side door at two minutes to twelve with the night still on his coat, and the front room is the tree and the television. Ma and his father are on the couch with Rosie asleep across both their laps, her feet on Frank and the wooden spoon still in her fist, and on the screen it’s Times Square for real this time, this year’s, with Dick Clark and Ryan Seacrest and the ball at the top of its pole. Gina is cross-legged on the rug with the Flip. Nonna is awake in her chair by the window, sitting up for it. Jack sits down on the rug beside Gina in his coat.

At a minute to, Ma gets up and turns the sound off and puts the record on the turntable in the console, as she has every year Jack can remember, the needle set down by hand, and is back on the couch before the ball starts down.

It comes down in silence, with the old band playing the old song out of the corner of the room. At zero his mother and father kiss over Rosie, quick, embarrassed by it, Frank’s hand coming up off Rosie’s ankle to Ma’s face and going straight back. Gina has the Flip on them. “*Regina*,” Ma says. “It’s *history*,” Gina says, and keeps filming, until Frank reaches over and puts his hand over the lens.

From the window Nonna says it. “*Buon anno.*” And then to each of them by name, one and the next, like beads: “Francesco. Maria. Regina. Rosaria” — who is asleep, and gets hers anyway — “Giacomino.” Then she looks past all of them at the wing chair by the stairs, where Danny watched the ball every year from the time he was old enough to stay up for the real one, and where nobody has sat tonight.
“Danny,” she says to it. “*Buon anno.*”
In his pocket the phone goes against his leg, three times, one after another, and he leaves it there till she’s done.
On the screen the year has gone up in confetti over a million people. His father watches it over Rosie’s feet.
“Twenty-ten,” Frank says. He tries it again. “Sounds like a year somebody builds a car.”

The record comes to the end of the song, and the needle runs on into the hiss. Ma gets up to see to it, and to the dishes after. Jack stays on the rug with his back against the couch and takes out the phone.

body: He answers Skye first. He knows he’s doing it while he does it, and he does it on purpose: in eight days he’ll be back in California, and after that they’re a thing with a name — January, that was the deal in the Saab — and a man answers that one first.
